quote.translation: Leibniz too drew the distinction between "absolute necessity" (nécessité absolue) and "hypothetical necessity" (nécessité hypothétique) (Leibniz, Opera philosophica, ed. Erdmann, p. 763), and according to Christian Wolff, "necessary existence is that whose existence is absolutely necessary (absolute necessaria); contingent existence is that which has the ground of its own existence outside itself", so that "the existence of contingent existence is merely hypothetically necessary (hypothetice necessaria)" (Christian Wolff, Ontologia, § 309f., § 316).

quote.translation: Kant too draws this distinction in the Lectures on Metaphysics: absolute necessity (absolute Notwendigkeit) is the case in which the existence of a thing is known a priori simply (simpliciter), and hypothetical necessity (hypothetische Notwendigkeit) the case in which the existence of a thing is known a priori according to something (secundum quid) (Kant's Vorlesungen über die Metaphysik, 2 Aufl. hrsg. v. Schmidt, S. 27).

quote.translation: This metaphysical contingency, which is merely hypothetically necessary, can also not exist, since, as Aristotle had already shown, it exists only through some cause other than itself, and this is why Thomas Aquinas calls the contingent "what is possible not to exist" (possibilia non esse) (Thomas Aquinas, Summa theologiae I. 2.

regions.text: それ故にトーマス・アクャナスは偶然を「存在しないことの可能のもの（possibilianonesse）」（ThomasAguinas,Summatheolosize【22）と呼んでるる。

quote.translation: Metaphysical contingency is, after all, nothing other than empirical necessity; yet even empirical necessity, insofar as it is witnessed over against the metaphysical necessity of the absolute, takes on the character of the contingent.

regions.text: 形而上約偶然は最意、経驗的必然にほかならないのであるが經驗的必然と難も絕對者の形而上的必然に對して目撃される限り偶然の性質を機びるのである。我々は趣驗的必然と原始個然との對立開係が原因結果の開係として假說的見地に於て成立し、形而上約偶然と超對的形而上約必然との對立開係が、全酸と部分との関係として、離接約見地に於て成立することを見た。

quote.translation: We have seen that the relation of opposition between empirical necessity and primal contingency holds, as the relation of cause and effect, at the hypothetical standpoint, and that the relation of opposition between metaphysical contingency and absolute metaphysical necessity holds, as the relation of whole and part, at the disjunctive standpoint.
We must next consider more closely the relation between primal contingency and absolute metaphysical necessity, and the relation between empirical necessity and metaphysical contingency.
